**A churn score identifies risk; a retention policy identifies useful action.** A user very likely to leave may not respond to any offer. Another user likely to stay may accept a discount they did not need. The relevant decision is which intervention changes the outcome enough to justify its cost.

**A numerical illustration.** Suppose an offer increases one user's estimated retention probability from 0.2 to 0.25 and another's from 0.6 to 0.8. The first user has greater churn risk, but the second has larger estimated treatment effect. If retained value and costs are comparable, the second may be the better target. These are illustrative conditional averages, not observable individual counterfactual truths. [3](https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook)

Collect randomized treatment/no-treatment data where feasible, with stable offer definitions and outcome windows. Train a policy on one set and evaluate it independently. Observational offer logs can be confounded because earlier teams deliberately targeted particular customers.

Optimize incremental retained value minus offer/contact cost, subject to eligibility and capacity. Include no action as a legitimate choice. Repeated discounts can alter future behavior, such as encouraging users to threaten cancellation, so short-term lift may not capture the long-term policy effect.

Check overlap, uncertainty, subgroup outcomes, and practical profitability. A sophisticated uplift model is not automatically better than a broad rule when treatment data is sparse or the intervention has little effect. Start with an experiment that establishes whether an offer works, then refine who receives it.

**Technical details and references.**

A churn model predicts who is likely to leave under the observed policy; a retention system needs to know whose outcome an intervention can change. Estimate treatment effects from randomized offers/contact experiments where possible, including a no-treatment control. High-risk users may be impossible to retain, while low-risk users may stay without a discount.

Choose actions by expected incremental retained value minus offer/contact cost, subject to eligibility, capacity, and fairness constraints. Treatment definitions and outcome windows must be stable. Uplift estimation requires overlap and valid causal assumptions; it is not automatically superior when treatment data are sparse, biased, or the intervention is ineffective.

Use separate data for policy learning and evaluation, and evaluate incremental profit/retention through experiments or justified off-policy methods. Monitor harms such as teaching users to threaten churn for discounts. A conservative fallback can use broad eligibility rules until treatment evidence accumulates. Report uncertainty and subgroup effects rather than presenting every individual uplift score as a known causal fact.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** For action a, compare expected incremental retained value $v(x)\tau_a(x)-cost_a(x)$ with the no-action baseline. Uplift estimates are conditional averages, not observable individual counterfactual truths. Validate the chosen policy on independent randomized data where possible, including uncertainty, offer capacity, and adverse behavioral effects of repeated incentives.
